passages.quote:
1. Introduction

The Rural Payments Agency (RPA) acts as the regulator for:

classifying beef, pig and sheep carcases

reporting market prices for certain categories of animals and carcases

labelling beef and veal products

The RPA does this in England on behalf of the Secretary of State for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), and in Wales on behalf of the Welsh Ministers.

The regulations, set out at section 8 of this document, aim to:

make sure producers are paid fairly based on the weight and composition of animals sent to slaughter

monitor and improve fairness and transparency in the market

ensure beef and veal can always be traced back to where it came from

These regulations apply to slaughterhouses and meat cutting plants. They support producers by making the deadweight supply chain clearer and more transparent.

The beef and veal labelling regulations protect consumers. They make sure the beef and veal sold match the description and country of origin on the label and is not a substitute product.

This guidance explains both:

the RPA’s approach to the legislation as the regulator

what actions and penalties the RPA can use

In this guidance, ‘we’ refers to the RPA or another party acting on behalf of the Secretary of State for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs, or the Welsh Ministers.

2. The RPA’s regulatory approach

The RPA’s approach is to prevent problems rather than fix them later. Our first step is to advise, guide and educate slaughterhouse operators to help them comply with the regulations. If this does not work, we will use our legal powers to make sure the regulations are complied with. There may also be some circumstances where advice and guidance alone is not appropriate.

Our approach and the use of civil and criminal powers follows the Regulators’ Code and the Better Regulation Principles. We focus on:

acting in proportion to the issue

being consistent

using risk-based activity

supporting people to comply with the regulations

The Regulators’ Code explains how regulators should work with slaughterhouse operators.

RPA Regulators’ Code shows how the RPA meets the 6 standards of the code to make sure we are open and fair with slaughterhouse operators.

The Better Regulation Framework guidance explains how officials must meet the Better Regulation Framework to make sure the regulations are checked and considered.

The RPA also follows the:

Home Office Code of Practice on Powers of Entry

Defra enforcement policy statement, in relation to England

3. The RPA’s outcome focused regulatory approach

The RPA works with slaughterhouse operators to make sure they comply with the regulations. We usually provide advice and guidance first. Where this is not appropriate, we take prompt enforcement action. This means the formal steps we can take to make sure the regulations are followed, including the use of civil or criminal powers.

We take appropriate actions to help those who need to comply with the regulations including:

issuing targeted communications such as timely reminders, hints and tips, and advice and guidance where it is needed

regularly checking how well our approach works and improve it if needed

using risk-based actions to reduce unnecessary work for those we regulate

4. What advice and guidance the RPA can give

The RPA advise, guide and support slaughterhouse operators to comply with the regulations.

If you commit a regulatory breach but it is not serious enough for us to use penalties, we will remind you of the regulations in writing. This gives you a chance to put things right without any penalties being applied.

A breach may be less serious due to one of the following (the list is not in priority order and is not exhaustive):

it’s a first offence or you usually meet the rules

the offence is small or has little impact

you admitted the offence and will work with us to fix it

If later evidence shows the offence is more serious, we may take stronger action including civil or criminal proceedings.

We may also offer advice and guidance where:

you have not broken any rules

you ask for advice and guidance

we think it will help prevent a future offence

We keep records of your compliance history including any advice given either verbally or in writing.

5. The RPA’s investigation powers - power of entry

The regulations give the RPA officers the right to enter premises to check if either:

any breach of the regulations has been committed

there is evidence of a breach

When an officer enters any premises, they may:

inspect, photograph or record a carcase or part of it

inspect, copy or print documents, records or materials related to the regulations, or remove them either to copy them or keep them as evidence

inspect, photograph and check machines, computers or equipment used under the regulations

require copies of documents, records or materials in a form to take away

6. Notices and penalties the RPA can use

If you breach the regulations, the RPA may send you a warning letter. We also have 4 forms of enforcement we can use.

1. Stop Notice (beef and veal labelling only)

Where beef or veal has been labelled or marketed incorrectly, we can issue a Stop Notice. This means the beef or veal must be either:

relabelled or removed from sale until it meets the regulations

is made into a product that does not need to meet the regulations

We may take stronger action if you do not follow the Stop Notice. This may lead to prosecution.

2. Compliance or Enforcement Notice

We may send a written Compliance or Enforcement Notice if an RPA officer believes a breach of the regulations has taken place. If you do not follow this notice, we may send you a Penalty Notice.
